rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1, 5 - field experiment with the fuzzy-IoT controller on apple trees in eastern Morocco, 10 days in summer 2022 and 10 days in winter 2023, with own sensor, flow-meter and energy measurements.
rows.notes: The study reports its own result on water saving (about 61% less water than a timer-controlled plot, Section 5.3) and on the controller withholding irrigation during high ET and rainfall (Sections 5.1, 5.2). It does not evaluate climate-change adaptation, resilience or risk reduction (no drought-year, yield-stability or vulnerability outcome). Water saving is a precondition of the adaptation/resilience effect the passage attributes to smart irrigation, so Q2 is no and upstream is set.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1, 5 - own field experiment in eastern Morocco (zones A and B, ~1300 m2 each, apple trees), 10 days summer 2022 and 10 days winter 2023. Q2: Section 5.3 - the SPIS-controlled zone A applied 51.6 mm versus 110 mm applied by the farmer with a commercial timer in zone B, a water saving of nearly 61% over 10 days, measured by a flow meter at the valve (Section 2.4). Q4: Section 5.1 and Fig. 14(d), 17(d) - the intermediate variable, soil moisture, is measured hourly and tracks the 30% target with smooth oscillations; irrigation durations logged against temperature and solar irradiance (Fig. 14b, 14c, 16) show irrigation withheld during high-ET periods and rainfall; applied depth (5.29 mm/day) compared with Penman-Monteith ET (5.31 mm/day). Q8: Section 2.2.1 - authors state that a single soil-moisture sensor was used and that further investigations subdividing the field are planned to ensure the generalizability of the results across the whole field. Q9: Section 5.3 - water saving reported as nearly 61% (<U+00B1>2%).
rows.notes: Q3: the saving rests on one method (flow-meter water volumes in the two zones); the ET comparison is a plausibility check, not an independent determination of the saving. Q5/Q6: one field, one crop, one site, plot scale (~100 m2 irrigated). Q7: no condition for the saving is stated as a requirement; the comparison is against a farmer-set timer applying 11 mm/day. Q8: the limitation stated concerns sensor coverage/generalizability of results across the field; the short 10-day duration and single comparison plot are not explicitly acknowledged as limitations. Q9: the <U+00B1>2% is given without explanation of how it was derived.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1, 5 - own field experiment with the fuzzy-IoT controller on apple trees in eastern Morocco, 20 days of monitoring across two seasons.
rows.notes: The study reports no yield, growth, fruit quality or any crop-productivity measurement. It only shows that soil moisture was maintained near the 30% threshold (Figs. 14d, 17d) and asserts, without data, that this keeps plants unstressed and ensures optimal growth (Sections 5.1, 5.3). Maintaining soil moisture is a precondition of the claimed productivity effect, so Q2 is no and upstream is set. Own results on water saving (61%) and energy saving (46%) are reported but concern other claims.

notes: Full text appears complete. Single-site, single-crop (apple) engineering field test with 10-day evaluation windows in two seasons; no replication, no statistics beyond a <U+00B1>2% on the water saving, no yield data.
